lesson.title: The Trickle Every Input Needs
lesson.summary: The input terminals of a real op-amp draw small bias currents to bias their internal input transistors, and those currents flowing through external resistors create additional DC output errors that the ideal model ignores.
lesson.body:
The ideal op-amp model assumes its inputs draw exactly zero current. That is a useful simplification for circuit analysis, but every real op-amp input is the base or gate of a transistor, and biasing that transistor into its active region requires some small current to actually flow into (or out of) each input pin. The average of the two input currents is called the input bias current, Ib. On op-amps with bipolar-transistor input stages, Ib is typically in the tens to hundreds of nanoamps. On op-amps with FET or CMOS input stages, it can be a thousand times smaller, down in the picoamp range. The two input currents are rarely perfectly equal either; the difference between them is called the input offset current, Ios, and it is normally much smaller than Ib itself.

Bias current becomes a real error source the moment it flows through a resistor, because current through a resistor makes a voltage. Consider an inverting amplifier with a feedback resistor Rf = 100 kΩ, built with an op-amp whose input bias current is Ib = 80 nA, a realistic value for an older bipolar-input general-purpose part. That bias current has to flow from the summing junction through Rf, and the voltage it develops across Rf shows up directly as an output error: Ib x Rf = 80 x 10^-9 A x 100 x 10^3 Ω = 8 x 10^-3 V, or 8 mV. So with the input signal at zero, the output sits 8 mV away from where the ideal model says it should be, purely because of bias current flowing through the feedback path.

There is a well-known fix. Add a resistor from the non-inverting input to ground with a value equal to the parallel combination of Rf and the source resistance feeding the inverting input. With that resistor in place, both inputs see roughly equal resistance to their respective reference points, so the (nearly equal) bias currents at each input produce nearly equal voltage drops, and those drops largely cancel in the amplifier's differential output. What remains after this compensation is a much smaller error driven by Ios rather than Ib, since the compensation only cancels the part of the two bias currents that matches.

Bias current error and offset voltage error, from the previous chapter, are independent effects and they add together at the output rather than canceling each other: total DC output error is approximately Vos x (noise gain) plus the residual bias-current term after any compensation. When precision matters, both need budgeting. Choosing a modern FET or CMOS input op-amp makes the bias current term nearly negligible, which is one reason those parts dominate in high-impedance sensor interfaces, but it does nothing about Vos, which stays the harder error to eliminate and usually the one that dominates a precision DC design.
